messages.subject: Fwd: Re: [stan-dev] profiling tools?
parts:
Let me rephrase the question. (And then I hope
someone else can use the answer to help Jiqiang
with problems on autocorrelation and autocovariance
because it's blocking his progress on RStan and I'm
going out of town; if the problem's still there in
two weeks, I'll take it up again.)

Can anyone point me to step-by-step instructions
on how to do profile g++ on the Mac? Everything I've
found either (a) doesn't work (like gprof under gcc),
or (b) looks horrendously complex (like Shark
under Xcode).

Here's what I'm doing in gprof, if anyone can tell
me where I'm going wrong.

Step 1: A really simple program with a function
call (in case error was that main() was invisible,
that takes enough time it shouldn't return 0 (in case
that was the problem)):

-----------------
#include <iostream>
int foo() {
double sum;
for (size_t j = 0; j < 1000; ++j) {
for (size_t i = 0; i < 1000000; ++i) {
sum += i;
}
if (j % 100 == 0) std::cout << "sum=" << sum << std::endl;
}
}

int main() {
foo();
}
---------------

~/stan> g++ -pg -g -o simple simple.cpp

~/stan> ls gmon.out
ls: gmon.out: No such file or directory

~/stan> ./simple
sum=5e+11
sum=5.04999e+13
sum=1.005e+14
sum=1.505e+14
sum=2.005e+14
sum=2.505e+14
sum=3.005e+14
sum=3.505e+14
sum=4.005e+14
sum=4.505e+14

~/stan> ls -l gmon.out
-rw-r--r-- 1 colloquialdotcom staff 912445 Jul 25 15:54 gmon.out

~/stan> gprof simple

Nada. Nyet. Bupkis. Just a bunch of empty forms. Ditto if I just
call "gprof" as some tutorials said. Ditto if I call gprof -f foo, etc.

I get the same thing if I run autocorrelation in Stan. There
were warnings about functions that were too fast, only called library
functions, etc.

Also various threads about gprof being broken on Mac OS X since 1996.

- Bob

P.S. Yes, I realize we should do this at -O3 when we care, but I can't
even manage to get simple profiling output.

messages.author: ab7b24da45678eac
messages.subject: Re: Re: [stan-dev] profiling tools?
parts:
The last answer on this page http://stackoverflow.com/questions/1101545/problem-with-gprof-on-os-x-program-is-not-of-the-host-architecture
says gprof is not working on mac.  Instead, using Shark in Xcode. 

I tried gprof on linux, which seems give me some results.  I could dig in more on this issue. 

In addition, repost what I said about the effective sample size just to say that this has nothing to do with R. 

To demonstrate that, I added a fake test as follows, which needs 131138ms to finish
on my computer. 

TEST(McmcChains,effective_sample_size) {
  std::vector<std::string> names;
  std::vector<std::vector<size_t> > dimss;
  stan::mcmc::read_variables("src/test/mcmc/test_csv_files/8schools1.csv", 3,
                             names, dimss);

  stan::mcmc::chains<> c(4, names, dimss);
  add_chain(c, 0, "src/test/mcmc/test_csv_files/8schools1.csv", 3);
  add_chain(c, 1, "src/test/mcmc/test_csv_files/8schools2.csv", 3);
  add_chain(c, 2, "src/test/mcmc/test_csv_files/8schools2.csv", 3);
  add_chain(c, 3, "src/test/mcmc/test_csv_files/8schools2.csv", 3);

  size_t index = 0;
  EXPECT_NEAR(13.08, c.effective_sample_size(index), 0.01) <<
    "the first sample size should be 13.1";
}

--
Jiqiang

them running unless you have an expert next to you.

> to say that this has nothing to do with R.

Thanks for the sample code. That certainly shows
the issue's not with R. I forgot how much other I/O
was going on on the Stan side. The issue has to
be in read_variables or add_chain because the FFT
comps for autocorrelation are fast.

It'd be nice to see where the bottlenecks were in the
code, but it might be obvious from inspection.

We can't have ESS taking two minutes to run for 8 schools!

- Bob

P.S. Daniel's also going to work on getting the one-chain
ESS working. We just need to make sure we scold the user

Jiqiang,

I highly recommend checking out kcachegrind for the profiling under Linux.  It's pretty easy to use, doesn't require recompiling everything with -pg and is prepackaged on practically every modern Linux distro.  Also, unlike gprof, it produces line-by-line (instead of function-by-function) statistics of where time is spent and its instrumentation doesn't tend skew timing results the same way gprof does.

I can dig up more specific directions if you would like them.

Cheers,
Marcus

FFTW (which Matlab uses) absolutely does not exhibit behavior like that.

I believe there should be a way to pad to a power of 2. It may just
work, but if not, there's probably some simple (to implement, once
found) correction.

How to use Instruments under Lion:
1. Fire up Instruments.
2. Select "CPU" under "Mac OS X" on the left side, and "Time Profiler"
on the right side.
3. Start the process you want to profile.
4. Select that process from the "Target" drop down in the upper left.
5. Hit the red "Record" button.
6. After a while, hit the record button again.
7. Profit.

Matt
